title: Maturity, Harvesting and Value Addition of Crops and Livestock

lessons.title: Maturity and harvesting decisions
lessons.html:
Maturity and harvesting decisions

The timing of harvest or marketing affects yield, quality, price and storage life. A manager must understand maturity indicators, plan harvest logistics and protect quality from the field to the buyer.

Crop maturity

CropMaturity indicators
MaizeBlack layer at kernel base (physiological maturity); harvest when grain moisture suits the harvester and storage or drying capacity
WheatGolden colour, hard kernels, grain moisture
Soya beansPods brown and dry, leaves dropped
Citrus, grapesColour, sugar (Brix), acid ratio set by export or market standards
VegetablesSize, firmness, head compactness, market specification

Grain harvested too wet needs drying and risks mould and mycotoxins; left too long it suffers shattering, lodging, weather damage and bird losses. Fresh produce harvested too early lacks flavour; too late it has short shelf life.

Livestock readiness for market

  • Weaners sold at weaning to feedlots: target weight and condition.
  • Slaughter stock: carcass weight, fat cover and age class, which drive the price under the carcass classification system used at abattoirs.
  • Lambs: live weight and condition for the target market.
  • Culls: old or unproductive animals sold before they lose condition in winter.

Withdrawal periods for any treatments must be over before animals are slaughtered or products sold. The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 requires slaughter at registered abattoirs for meat sold to the public.

Harvest planning

  • Book contractors, trucks, labour and storage in advance.
  • Prepare and service harvesters, bins and dryers.
  • Plan for weather risk and grain grading requirements.
  • Plan livestock handling: gathering, sorting, weighing and humane transport in line with the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

lessons.title: Post-harvest handling and adding value
lessons.html:
Post-harvest handling and adding value

Post-harvest handling

  • Grain: clean, dry to safe storage moisture, store in clean, sealed silos or bags; monitor temperature and insects; grade to the buyer's standards.
  • Fresh produce: harvest in the cool of the day, shade in the field, pre-cool quickly, maintain the cold chain, grade and pack to specification.
  • Livestock: minimise stress before slaughter; avoid bruising in handling and transport, which lowers carcass value.
  • Milk: cool quickly and keep cold to preserve quality.

Post-harvest losses in fruit and vegetables can be large. Most are caused by mechanical damage, heat and delays, all of which management can control.

Value addition options

OptionExamples
Grading and packingSelling graded, packed vegetables to retailers rather than ungraded to hawkers
StorageHolding grain to sell later in the season when prices may be higher
ProcessingMilling maize meal, making cheese or yoghurt, drying fruit, making biltong
Finishing livestockFeeding own grain to weaners to sell heavier animals
CertificationOrganic, GLOBALG.A.P. or other standards for export or premium markets
Direct marketingFarm stall, markets, local shops, online orders

Evaluating value addition

Value addition is worthwhile only if the extra income exceeds the extra costs and risks. Consider:

  • capital for equipment and facilities;
  • food safety compliance and labelling regulations for processed foods;
  • additional labour and skills;
  • market demand, competition and price premiums;
  • storage costs, interest and price risk for stored grain.

Example: storing 100 t of maize for four months is attractive only if the expected price increase covers storage fees, interest on the money, insurance and quality risk.

Key points

  • Harvest at the right maturity using crop-specific indicators.
  • Market livestock at target weight and condition, after withdrawal periods.
  • Plan harvest logistics, storage and humane livestock handling in advance.
  • Control post-harvest losses through cooling, gentle handling and speed.
  • Add value only where extra income exceeds extra costs and risks.
